description: The agent's vocabulary for the conventions of scientific prose — what definitions look like, how theorems are stated, how citations work, the IMRaD structure, hedging conventions. Foundational to extracting structured claims from research text.

concepts.name: definitional_sentence
concepts.definition: A sentence introducing a term and stating what it refers to. In math, conventionally marked by 'Definition.', 'Define', 'Let X be ...', 'X is called a ...'. Body after the marker defines the term.

concepts.name: theorem_statement
concepts.definition: A sentence (or block) asserting a proved result. Marked by 'Theorem.', often with author/year. Body asserts a conditional or universal claim. Followed by a Proof. block.

concepts.name: lemma_statement
concepts.definition: A sentence (or block) asserting an auxiliary result, typically used in service of a main theorem. Conventions identical to theorem_statement.

concepts.name: corollary_statement
concepts.definition: A sentence (or block) asserting an immediate consequence of a preceding theorem. Often with brief or no proof.

concepts.name: proposition_statement
concepts.definition: A sentence (or block) asserting a result less central than a theorem but more substantive than a lemma. Conventions identical to theorem_statement.

concepts.name: conjecture_statement
concepts.definition: A sentence asserting a proposed result that is plausible but unproved. Marked by 'Conjecture.', 'It is conjectured that ...'. The substrate should NOT take conjectures as established facts.

concepts.name: proof_step
concepts.definition: One sentence in a proof, typically connected to surrounding steps by inference markers ('Since', 'By X', 'Thus'). Carries an intermediate inference.

concepts.name: proof_completion_marker
concepts.definition: A symbol or phrase marking the end of a proof. 'QED', the open box, 'square root of two squared', 'This completes the proof.'

concepts.name: citation_year_author
concepts.definition: Inline citation of the form 'Author (Year)' or 'Author, Year' or '(Author Year)'. The standard mechanism for grounding a claim in prior published work.

concepts.name: citation_bracketed_number
concepts.definition: Inline citation of the form '[12]' referring to a bibliography entry. Common in CS / engineering.

concepts.name: citation_doi
concepts.definition: A DOI (digital object identifier) string, usually following an author-year citation. Provides a stable resolvable identifier for the cited work.

concepts.name: abstract_section
concepts.definition: Opening section of a paper summarizing its contribution. Typically 100-300 words. The first place to look for the paper's main claim.

concepts.name: introduction_section
concepts.definition: Section motivating the work, surveying prior work, stating the contribution. Often heaviest in citations.

concepts.name: methods_section
concepts.definition: Section describing the procedure / construction / proof technique used. The 'how' of the paper.

concepts.name: results_section
concepts.definition: Section presenting the main findings — theorems proved, experiments completed, data observed.

concepts.name: discussion_section
concepts.definition: Section interpreting the results — what they mean, what they don't show, what's next.

concepts.name: conclusion_section
concepts.definition: Closing section restating the contribution and pointing to future work. Often a good place to find the paper's bottom-line claim.

concepts.name: hedging
concepts.definition: Linguistic marking of partial commitment — 'may', 'might', 'suggests', 'tends to', 'apparently'. Signals the speaker is not fully confident in the claim.

concepts.name: certainty_marker
concepts.definition: Linguistic marking of full commitment — 'clearly', 'obviously', 'we prove', 'it is known that'. Signals the speaker stands fully behind the claim.

concepts.name: qualification
concepts.definition: A restriction on the scope of a claim — 'for n >= 3', 'in the planar case', 'assuming the axiom of choice'. Critical for accurate extraction.

concepts.name: forward_reference
concepts.definition: An in-text pointer to material yet to come — 'see Theorem 3 below', 'we will show'. Indicates the cited claim isn't proved at this point.

concepts.name: backward_reference
concepts.definition: An in-text pointer to material already presented — 'by Theorem 2', 'as shown above', '(*)' referring to a numbered equation.

concepts.name: equation_inline
concepts.definition: A mathematical expression appearing within a paragraph, surrounded by $...$ or \(...\). Compact, part of the sentence flow.

concepts.name: equation_display
concepts.definition: A mathematical expression set apart on its own line(s), surrounded by $$...$$ or \[...\] or in an equation environment. Highlights a key formula.

concepts.name: equation_numbered
concepts.definition: A display equation labeled with a number for cross-reference. The label is the equation's identity in subsequent references.

concepts.name: named_result
concepts.definition: A theorem with a conventional name — 'the Halting Theorem', 'Fermat's Last Theorem', 'Theorem of Najman'. Named results are particularly important for the substrate to recognize.

concepts.name: open_problem
concepts.definition: A statement that some question remains unanswered. Marked by 'is open', 'remains unknown', 'whether X is unknown'. The substrate should not assume an answer exists.

rules.name: a_definitional_sentence_introduces_a_term_and_its_body_defines_it
if: a Sentence is a definitional_sentence (starts with Definition., Define, Let, Suppose, or 'X is called')
then: the term to be defined appears immediately after the marker
the body after 'is' or '=' is the definition
the substrate may install the (term, definition) as a Concept node
rules.why: Definitions are the most reliable source of substrate-grade Concept material in research text.

rules.name: a_theorem_statement_asserts_an_if_then_claim
then: the body of the theorem is conventionally an if/then conditional (possibly with universal quantification)
the substrate may install the (hypothesis, conclusion) as a Rule node
rules.why: Theorems in standard form ARE Rules in the substrate's sense. The conversion is direct.

rules.name: a_citation_grounds_a_claim_in_prior_work
if: a Sentence contains a citation_year_author or citation_bracketed_number
then: the Sentence's claim is attributed to the cited work, not to the current author
the cited work is the authoritative source if the claim needs verification
rules.why: Distinguishing original claims from cited claims affects how the substrate treats them — original claims are the paper's contribution; cited claims are background.

rules.name: a_doi_uniquely_identifies_the_cited_work
then: the DOI is the canonical identifier for the cited work
the agent may fetch the full text by resolving the DOI
rules.why: DOIs are the substrate's hook for autonomous citation following — they're machine-resolvable identifiers.

rules.name: a_qualification_restricts_the_scope_of_a_claim
if: a Sentence contains a qualification ('for n >= 3', 'in the planar case')
then: the claim applies ONLY within the qualification's scope
matching the claim against a question requires checking the question falls in scope
rules.why: Unqualified extraction of a qualified claim produces wrong answers. The substrate must honor qualifications.

rules.name: hedging_signals_reduced_speaker_commitment
then: the claim is not fully asserted; the substrate should reduce its confidence accordingly
downstream reasoning should treat the claim as a candidate hypothesis, not as established fact
rules.why: Treating hedged claims as facts inflates the substrate's confidence and produces wrong answers.

rules.name: an_open_problem_means_no_answer_is_currently_known
if: a Sentence states a problem is open
then: the substrate should NOT extract a claim about the open problem's answer
any apparent answer in the text is a conjecture, not a fact
rules.why: Open problems are the right place to halt extraction; pretending an answer exists corrupts the knowledge base.

rules.name: a_proof_step_carries_one_inference_in_a_proof_chain
if: a Sentence is in a proof block AND starts with a premise marker ('Since', 'By', 'Because')
then: the Sentence carries one step of the proof inference
extracting the full proof requires composing the steps
rules.why: Proof chains are the textual form of the substrate's rule-application sequences.

rules.name: an_abstract_section_summarizes_the_paper_contribution
if: a Sentence is in the abstract_section
then: the Sentence likely encodes the paper's main claim or contribution
the substrate should rank abstract sentences highly for paper-level questions
rules.why: The abstract is the densest, highest-priority source of the paper's headline claim.
